fetched_contents.text: A continuous measure of phasic electrodermal activity Abstract Electrodermal activity is characterized by the superposition of what appear to be single distinct skin conductance responses (SCRs). Classic trough-to-peak analysis of these responses is impeded by their apparent superposition. A deconvolution approach is proposed, which separates SC data into continuous signals of tonic and phasic activity. The resulting phasic activity shows a zero baseline, and overlapping SCRs are represented by predominantly distinct, compact impulses showing an average duration of less than 2 s. A time integration of the continuous measure of phasic activity is proposed as a straightforward indicator of event-related sympathetic activity. The quality and benefit of the proposed measure is demonstrated in an experiment with short interstimulus intervals as well as by means of a simulation study. The advances compared to previous decomposition methods are discussed. Keywords: EDA, SC, GSR, Deconvolution, Decomposition, Phasic, Tonic, Integration, Sudomotor activity 1. Introduction Electrodermal activity (EDA) refers to the variation of the electrical properties of the skin in response to sweat secretion. By applying a low constant voltage, the change in skin conductance (SC) can be measured non-invasively (Fowles et al., 1981). This easy acquisition and the exclusive innervation of the sweat glands by the sympathetic nervous system contribute to the wide application of SC measures in basic as well as clinical research (Dawson et al., 2007). Sudomotor activity plays a major role in thermoregulation (Wenger, 2003) and in keeping the skin flexible for sensory discrimination (Jänig, 2006), but it is also a concomitant of the orienting response and more general of emotional arousal (Boucsein, 1992). Clinical application encompasses a variety of fields, such as the assessment of pain (e.g., Ledowski et al., 2007; Storm, 2008), schizophrenia (e.g., Raine et al., 1999; Yamamoto and Hornykiewicz, 2004) or peripheral neuropathy (e.g., Polo et al., 2000; Torigoe et al., 1999). The activity of sweat glands is triggered by postganglionic sudomotor fibers. Each sweat gland is innervated by many different sudomotor fibers (Kennedy et al., 1994; Riedl et al., 1998) and each sudomotor fiber innervates a skin area of about 1.28 cm2 (Schmelz et al., 1998). The average firing rate of sudomotor fibers was assessed as 0.62 Hz (Macefield and Wallin, 1996). The temporal concurrence in the firing of multiple fibers is identified as a nerve burst in the integrated nerve record; however, single fibers usually contribute only one single spike to each nerve burst (Macefield and Wallin, 1996). A sudomotor nerve burst corresponds to an observable skin conductance response (SCR). The spike density (as reflected by the amplitude of the nerve burst in the integrated nerve record) is linearly related to the number of recruited sweat glands (Freedman et al., 1994; Nishiyama et al., 2001) and to the amplitude of the corresponding SCR (Bini et al., 1980; Lidberg and Wallin, 1981). The SCR amplitude can therefore be considered as an index of sympathetic activity. The time series of SC can be characterized by a slowly varying tonic activity (i.e., skin conductance level; SCL) and a fast varying phasic activity (i.e., SCRs). SCRs may reflect stimulus-specific responses or non-specific responses. An SCR shows a steep incline to the peak and a slow decline to the baseline. The succession of SCRs usually results in a superposition of subsequent SCRs, as one SCR arises on top of the declining trail of the preceding one. In empirical research, it is a common procedure to assess the event-related activity to a given stimulus or intervention by gauging the amplitude of the elicited SCRs. The standard peak detection method (trough-to-peak) defines the SCR amplitude as the difference of the SC values at its peak and at the preceding trough (Boucsein, 1992; Edelberg, 1967). SCRs which occur in a predefined response window (typically 1–3 s or 1–5 s after the stimulus) are attributed to the stimulus (Dawson et al., 2007; Levenson and Edelberg, 1985). Additionally, a minimum amplitude criterion (e.g., 0.05 μS) is often applied. This scoring technique, however, can be complicated in the case of closely superposing SCRs. Presuming an additive superposition of subsequent SCRs, the shape of an SCR could be altered by the trails of preceding phasic activity (Boucsein, 1992). The degree of alteration would depend on the amplitude and proximity of preceding SCRs (Grings and Schell, 1969). For standard peak detection, the non-consideration of the declining trails of preceding activity is expected to result in an underestimation of the amplitude of subsequent SCRs. This methodological effect, which may cause artificial response attenuation, must not be confounded with potential refractory processes of the sweat gland, which may cause factual attenuation of later responses. However, experiments applying intraneural stimulation do not show significant response attenuation for repeated stimulation (Kunimoto et al., 1992a,b), which indicates that refractory processes may not have a strong impact on SCR amplitude. The issue of superposing responses motivated the proposal of several methodological developments aiming at more precise assessments of the SCR amplitude. Lim et al. (1997) proposed a curve-fitting method for the decomposition of 10-s segments of SC data. A four- to eight-parameter model accounts for the SCL, the slope of preceding phasic activity and the shape of one or two overlapping SCRs. After the appropriate model is determined by visual inspection of the respective data segment, the model will be fitted to the data using a least-squares method. Lim et al. Publication recommendations for electrodermal measurements. Psychophysiology, 49, 1017-1034. Boucsein, W (2012) Electrodermal activity (2nd Ed). New York: Springer. Critchley, H.D. (2010). Electrodermal Responses: What Happens in the Brain. The Neuroscientist, 8, 132-144. Dawson, ME, et al (2001) The Electrodermal System. In J. T. Cacioppo, L. G. Tassinary, and G.B. Bernston, (Eds) Handbook of Psychophysiology (2nd Ed), 200-223. Cambridge Press, Cambridge. Venables, PH, & Christie, MJ (1980). Electrodermal activity. In Martin, I & Venables, PH (Eds) Techniques in Psychophysiology, 3-67. Chichester, UK. Wiley. Nagai, Y., Critchley, H.D., Featherstone, E., Trimble, M.R., & Dolan, R.J., (2004). Activity in ventromedial prefrontal cortex covaries with sympathetic skin conductance level: a physiological account of a default mode of brain function, NeuroImage, 22, 243-251. Technology The BIOPAC MP36R is a state-of-the-art DAQ device. With specific reference to EDA, it produces exosomatic (DC) measures of skin conductance. It has 4-channels, each of which can be configured to sample up to 100,000samples/sec. It utilises a 24-bit A/D converter making it the fastest sampling and most sensitive device of its type currently available. The device is purely software configured (AcqKnowledge) and has no hardware setting-switches on it (other that the power switch to turn it on). It can be interfaced directly to a computer responsible for stimulus presentation so that EDA correlates of specific stimuli can be tagged and detected or it can be used in a more clinical and ambulatory setting merely gathering EDA measures in response to more general environmental / situational stimulation. All data can be analysed in AcqKnowledge and / or saved in formats of other leading packages for further extended analyses (e.g., Excel, Matlab). The existence of 4-channels means that EDA measurements can be simultaneously complemented by additional psychophysiological measures. Data from the MP36R can also be time-linked to concurrent video recordings, where both can be played-back in concert / parallel. This makes it particularly useful for clinical settings and patient-based neuropsychology. The MP36R can also be used as a 4- channel EEG and multiple devices can be linked together to provide more channels. 2 Section 1.1: Background Electrodermal activity (EDA) is the umbrella term used for defining autonomic changes in the electrical properties of the skin. The most widely studied property is the skin conductance, which can be quantified by applying an electrical potential between two points of skin contact and measuring the resulting current flow between them. The EDA complex includes both background tonic (skin conductance level: SCL) and rapid phasic components (Skin Conductance Responses: SCRs) that result from sympathetic neuronal activity. EDA is arguably the most useful index of changes in sympathetic arousal that are tractable to emotional and cognitive states as it is the only autonomic psychophysiological variable that is not contaminated by parasympathetic activity. EDA has been closely linked to autonomic emotional and cognitive processing, and EDA is a widely used as a sensitive index of emotional processing and sympathetic activity This coupling between cognitive states, arousal, emotion and attention enables EDA to be used as an objective index of emotional states. EDA can also be used to examine implicit emotional responses that may occur without conscious awareness or are beyond cognitive intent (i.e., threat, anticipation, salience, novelty). Recent research has shown that EDA is also a useful indicator of attentional processing per-se, where salient stimuli and resource demanding tasks evoke increased EDA responses. Investigations of EDA have also been used to illuminate wider areas of enquiry such as; psychopathology, personality disorders, conditioning, and neuropsychology. Recent improvements in technology, methodology and reporting have meant that EDA has become an increasingly important variable in psychological science. These improvements have also led to further refinements in analysis techniques and the methods used for handling EDA data and making it fit for final analysis and interpretation. Such advancements also leave room for some controversies over how EDA should be analysed in given circumstances. This document is designed primarily for use by non-experts in research on EDA. Introduction Electrodermal activity (EDA) is a non-stationary signal that indicates electrical potential via the sweat glands on the surface of the skin (Boucsein, 2012). EDA represents a quantitative functional measure of sudomotor activity and, therefore, an objective assessment of emotional arousal (Ellaway, Kuppuswamy, Nicotra, & Mathias, 2010). An EDA signal can be decomposed into two different and non-redundant components: a phasic and tonic component (Benedek & Kaernbach, 2010). The phasic component is the decomposition of the rapid movements of the signal, known as the skin conductance response (SCR), which commonly provides the features used in EDA-based studies to provide valuable information for many scientific research fields (Posada-Quintero & Chon, 2020). Special attention has been given to the approach by psychology and health-related studies (Dawson, Schell, & Filion, 2000). In clinical analysis, SCR is used to assess pain, stress, schizophrenia, and peripheral neuropathy (Benedek and Kaernbach, 2010, Ellaway et al., 2010). In neuroscience and psychology, it is used to assess the subject’s arousal levels (Greco, Valenza and Scilingo, 2016). For example, Anusha, Jose, Preejith, Jayaraj, and Mohanasankar (2018) used EDA signals to assess the stress of subjects in emulated real-life job scenarios, and Zangróniz, Martínez Rodrigo, Pastor García, López Bonal, and Fernández-Caballero (2017) studied EDA to distinguish between stressful and calm conditions. Liu and Du (2018) also analyzed the stress levels of a subject using the signal. Elsewhere, studies related to mental illness have utilized EDA signals, with Greco, Valenza, Lanatà, Rota, and Scilingo (2014) finding statistical evidence concerning the relationship between healthy patients and patients with bipolar disorder using features of EDA signals and Perugia et al. (2017) discovering significant correlations between EDA signals and engagement in dementia patients. Most previous research has collected EDA signals in laboratory environments (Shukla, Barreda-Ángeles, Oliver, & Puig, 2018), where subjects are usually seated and often cautioned not to move the hand to which the electrodes are attached. However, recent applications have recorded EDA in environments where the users can walk freely and move their hands, such as daily-life settings and virtual reality (VR) environments. Notably, many wearable devices have been developed to enable the possibility of acquiring EDA signals in a daily-life scenario, leading (Malathi, Jayaseeli, Madhuri, & Senthilkumar, 2018) to propose a wearable EDA sensor for detecting drowsiness in drivers, Leite, Henriques, Martinho, and Paiva (2013) to analyze the affective state of children in everyday situations when interacting with robots, and Kim and Fesenmaier (2015) to measure traveler emotions in real time during a four-day visit. Meanwhile, VR has been used to simulate environments where subjects can freely move and interact, which creates the sensation of being in the real world (Chicchi Giglioli, Pravettoni, Sutil, Parra, & Alcañiz Raya, 2017). VR can display different scenarios to evoke emotions or provoke cognitive processes in the subject (Marín-Morales et al., 2019, Raya et al., 2003) and has been used in case studies of, for example, social adaptation in social phobia contexts, the reduction of anxiety and pain, rehabilitation, and neurological diagnosis (Bekele et al., 2017, Li et al., 2011, Maskeliunas et al., 2019, Matijević et al., 2013, Tarrant et al., 2018). EDA has been used in VR experiments to examine sudomotor activity and arousal levels to assess anxiety and stress (Kritikos, Tzannetos, Zoitaki, Poulopoulou, & Koutsouris, 2019), conduct emotional assessments (Salgado et al., 2018), and diagnose autism (Alcañiz Raya et al., 2020). However, among the most significant issues concerning the use of EDA signals in daily-life and VR environments is the subject’s movement during data collection. Although these technologies can offer an accurate environment for recording subject responses, the absence of control over the environments can impact EDA records. Most movements can cause interferences in the contact between the skin and the recording electrodes, producing major artifacts in EDA recordings (Taylor et al., 2015). Shukla et al. (2018) suggested that artifacts in EDA signals may conceal the existence of important correlations between the signal and the subject’s arousal levels due to their heavy influence on the phasic component. Therefore, ensuring the quality of the signal in uncontrolled environments represents a critical challenge. Most EDA-based experiments manually remove major artifacts using a human expert, because there is no robust and established methodology for automatically recognizing and correcting EDA signals. Artifacts can be manually corrected using various software, including Ledalab (www.ledalab.de) and SCRalyze (Bach, 2014). However, manual correction has several disadvantages. First, it is a time-consuming and tedious task. Second, manual correction can introduce subjective human bias, with different experts correcting different signals. However, most critically, it cannot be applied in real-time or for short time periods without human intervention, as there is a demand for intelligent wearable devices that need to integrate a fully automated pipeline into the sensors. Examples of such systems include automatic systems for disorder recognition (Alcañiz Raya et al., 2020) adaptive therapies (Maskeliunas et al., 2019), mental health monitoring systems at home (Zangróniz et al., 2017), driver drowsiness detection (Malathi et al., 2018), and aesthetic evaluations (Marín-Morales et al., 2019). ## Typical timing characteristics of SCR in EDA studies

The literature describes phasic skin conductance responses (SCRs) as stereotyped waveforms with a steep rise, peak, and slow decline, but with superposition and contamination making exact timing parameters variable across studies and contexts [N1-F1]. In standard practice, SCRs are typically detected relative to a stimulus, and the amplitude is often defined as the difference between the peak and the preceding trough, with a commonly used response window of 1–3 or 1–5 seconds after stimulus onset [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that a minimum amplitude criterion, such as 0.05 μS, is often applied to identify meaningful responses [N1-F1].

### Common timing ranges reported in the literature
The evidence provided does not give a single canonical set of latency, amplitude, duration, rise time, and fall time values across all studies, but it does describe the general structure of SCRs and the metrics used to quantify them:

- **Latency**: The standard peak detection method defines SCR amplitude relative to the preceding trough, and latency is measured from stimulus onset to the first significant deviation in the signal [N2-R1]. A practical guide notes that ER-SCR latency is typically defined as the period between stimulus onset and the first significant deviation in the signal, and reports the common window as 1–3 seconds [N2-R1]. Biopac’s guide also mentions latency, SCR amplitude, rise time, size, and onset as metrics in SCR analysis [N4-R1]. The larger overview emphasizes that the standard trough-to-peak method defines amplitude as peak minus trough, and that SCRs may occur in a predefined response window of 1–3 s or 1–5 s after stimulus [N1-F1].

- **Amplitude**: The standard method defines amplitude as peak minus trough, and the practical guide notes that increased amplitude indicates a more intense response [N1-F1][N4-R4]. The Biopac guide also includes amplitude as a reported statistic [N4-R1].

- **Duration**: The evidence does not provide a fixed numerical range for SCR duration, but it does describe the waveform as an average duration of less than 2 seconds when deconvolved into continuous phasic activity [N1-F1]. In practical analysis, the response window used to detect SCRs (1–3 s or 1–5 s) implicitly defines the timing window for duration interpretation [N1-F1][N2-R1].

- **Rise time**: The evidence notes that rise time is a reported metric in SCR analysis [N4-R1], and it is associated with emotional arousal in the biorxiv study, where higher arousal was linked to shorter ER-SCR rise times [N4-R3].

- **Fall time**: The evidence does not give a direct numerical range for fall time, but it describes the SCR waveform as a steep incline to the peak and a slow decline to the baseline [N1-F1]. That slow decline is relevant to fall time interpretation.

### How SCR timing varies by stimulus type, task, and participant characteristics
The evidence suggests that SCR timing is context-dependent and therefore varies across stimulus type, task, and participants. First, the waveform can be altered by preceding phasic activity when responses overlap, with amplitude and proximity of earlier SCRs affecting the shape of later responses [N1-F1]. Second, the study design itself affects the timing window: SCRs are often attributed to a stimulus if the latency falls within a predefined window of 1–3 s or 1–5 s after stimulus onset [N1-F1]. Third, emotional arousal is tied to SCR timing: the biorxiv study found that higher arousal was associated with greater ER-SCR amplitudes and shorter ER-SCR rise times [N4-R3]. This indicates that task or experimental condition can change the timing profile.

The evidence also implies that participant characteristics matter. The waveform is described as stereotyped within-subject but variable across subjects, and the deconvolution approach is motivated by the need to separate overlapping responses, which is especially important when subjects differ in the frequency and timing of their sudomotor activity [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Thus, SCR timing is not a universal constant but depends on the participant’s autonomic response profile.

### What defines a valid SCR versus an artifact or false response
A valid SCR is one that is properly timed relative to the stimulus and meets a minimum amplitude criterion. The standard trough-to-peak method defines amplitude as peak minus trough, and SCRs occurring within a predefined window are attributed to the stimulus [N1-F1]. The practical guide also notes that latency is defined as the period between stimulus onset and the first significant deviation in the signal, which supports a time-based criterion for identifying event-related responses [N2-R1]. However, the same evidence warns that standard peak detection can underestimate amplitude when preceding trails are ignored, and that this can be confused with actual refractory processes [N1-F1].

Artifacts or false responses are not explicitly enumerated numerically in the provided evidence, but the methodological literature clearly frames them as contamination. The EDA signal is described as being built up of SCL, SCR, and artifacts, and automatic artifact detection is discussed as an important concern [N2-R3]. In real-world/ecological settings, movement can cause interference between skin and electrodes, producing major artifacts [N5-F4]. This suggests that a valid SCR must be distinguished from contamination or crosstalk by careful timing alignment, amplitude thresholding, and artifact screening. The evidence also notes that manual correction is still common but has limitations such as subjectivity and time consumption [N5-F4].

In summary, SCR timing in EDA studies is usually measured in a predefined time window around a stimulus, with latency, amplitude, rise time, and fall time reported as standard metrics [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-R1]. The same waveform can vary by stimulus, task, and participant, especially with emotional arousal affecting rise time and amplitude [N1-F1][N4-R3]. A valid SCR is one that falls within the stimulus window and meets a minimum amplitude criterion, while artifacts are contamination or crosstalk that must be excluded through careful detection and processing [N1-F1][N2-R3][N5-F4].

## Methodological considerations for SCR timing analysis

SCR timing analysis is highly sensitive to detection thresholds, signal processing choices, and artifact handling, all of which can distort timing accuracy and inflate or deflate the apparent response profile.

### Detection thresholds and signal processing choices that affect timing accuracy
The standard trough-to-peak method is central to SCR analysis, but it defines amplitude as the difference between peak and trough and does not account for the declining trails of preceding phasic activity [N1-F1]. This can lead to underestimation of subsequent SCRs, which is a methodological effect and should not be confused with refractory processes [N1-F1]. In practice, a minimum amplitude criterion is often applied, such as 0.05 μS, to identify meaningful responses [N1-F1]. The Biopac guide also explicitly lists latency, SCR amplitude, rise time, size, and onset as reported metrics, indicating that timing is not determined in isolation but in conjunction with other waveform features [N4-R1].

Signal processing choices matter because the waveform is often decomposed into tonic and phasic components, and the phasic component is modeled as a linear convolution between sudomotor sympathetic activity and the skin response [N1-R4]. The same source describes a deconvolution approach that separates SC data into continuous tonic and phasic activity, with the phasic activity represented by compact impulses averaging less than 2 seconds in duration [N1-F1]. This suggests that the choice of decomposition method can alter how timing is extracted. The evidence also notes that curve-fitting methods can improve amplitude and latency estimates compared to standard trough-to-peak methods [N1-F1]. Thus, the choice of detection algorithm, windowing, and decomposition can change timing estimates.

### Handling of baseline drift, noise, and movement artifacts
Baseline drift and noise are important because they can obscure the SCR waveform. The standard peak detection method assumes a baseline, and the evidence warns that ignoring preceding trails can produce an artificial attenuation effect [N1-F1]. In real-world and ecologically valid studies, movement is a major concern. The automatic artifact recognition paper notes that motion can produce major artifacts in EDA recordings, and recent work on motion artifact detection and correction explores automated pipelines [N5-F4]. The same source explains that movement can interfere with skin-electrode contact, creating artifacts that may conceal important correlations between EDA and arousal [N5-F4]. This implies that baseline drift and noise can be handled by careful signal processing and artifact detection, while movement artifacts require dedicated correction.

### How to distinguish true responses from contamination or crosstalk
The evidence explicitly separates the EDA signal into three components: skin conductance level (SCL), skin conductance response (SCR), and artifacts [N2-R3]. This distinction is central to identifying true responses. Artifacts can be difficult to remove because manual correction is still common but limited by subjectivity, time, and the inability to do it in real time [N5-F4]. The automatic artifact recognition paper describes a machine learning algorithm for detecting EDA artifacts and provides empirical evaluation, while another study develops a fully automatic pipeline for recognizing and correcting motion EDA artifacts [N5-R1][N5-R2]. These developments show that distinguishing true responses from contamination requires both automated detection and manual oversight.

The practical guide also emphasizes that EDA signals are analyzed using software such as AcqKnowledge and that signal processing and handling are integral to the analysis pipeline [N4-F3]. It also notes that the signal can be time-linked to concurrent video recordings and used in clinical or ambulatory settings, which increases the likelihood of contamination from movement or environmental factors [N4-F3]. In short, a true SCR is one that is properly timed relative to a stimulus, has sufficient amplitude, and is not contaminated by baseline drift, noise, or movement artifacts. Contamination or crosstalk is indicated when the waveform deviates from the expected SCR profile or when automated/artifact detection identifies a signal change that is not a genuine sudomotor response [N2-R3][N5-F4].

## Study design and analysis considerations for SCR timing

SCR timing analysis depends on whether the study is stimulus-locked, within-trial, or between-trial, and each approach has different implications for within-subject and between-subject comparisons.

### Time-locked versus within-trial versus between-trial analysis approaches
Event-related skin conductance responses are traditionally analyzed by comparing the amplitude of individual peaks against a pre-stimulus baseline [N3-R1]. The Biopac guide similarly states that both latency and SCR amplitude together provide a time window for identifying event-related SCRs, and that if the measured latency falls within the window, the SCR is attributed to the stimulus [N3-R2]. This supports the time-locked approach as the standard method for stimulus-locked SCRs [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The same guide also notes that SCRs are sometimes time-anchored to predefined workflow events, which reinforces the idea that time-locked analysis is useful when events are well-defined [N3-R3].

Within-trial analysis is less explicitly described in the provided evidence, but the general discussion of waveform structure and superposition implies that trial-to-trial variation can be large, especially when multiple SCRs overlap [N1-F1]. The evidence also discusses modeling SCR time series during an experiment and event-related responses time-locked to each trial [N6-R3]. This suggests that within-trial analysis can be used to examine trial-level dynamics, but it may be more challenging because each trial may contain multiple overlapping responses or no clear response at all.

Between-trial analysis is implied by the comparison of SCRs across trials, where amplitude, latency, and other metrics can vary depending on the trial’s context [N1-F1][N3-R3]. The evidence also notes that in some studies, SCRs are analyzed as event-locked responses time-anchored to trial events, which supports between-trial comparison when stimuli or tasks are repeated across trials [N3-R3].

### Within-subject and between-subject comparison issues
The evidence emphasizes that SCR timing is not uniform across subjects. The waveform is described as stereotyped within-subject but variable across subjects [N1-R3]. This is important because within-subject comparisons can be more reliable than between-subject comparisons if the subject’s baseline and response profile are consistent. The same source also notes that the average firing rate of sudomotor fibers is 0.62 Hz, which is relevant because individual differences in sudomotor activity can produce different SCR timing profiles [N1-F1]. The Biopac guide further stresses that EDA signals are analyzed using software such as AcqKnowledge and that the signal can be time-linked to concurrent recordings, which supports within-subject tracking of SCR timing [N4-F3].

Between-subject comparisons are complicated by the fact that SCR timing and amplitude can differ systematically by participant. The evidence does not provide a direct numerical comparison of mean differences, but it does note that the standard trough-to-peak method can underestimate amplitude when preceding trails are ignored, and that this effect can be confounded with refractory processes [N1-F1]. This implies that between-subject comparisons should be cautious about interpreting differences as purely physiological, because they may reflect methodological or individual differences in response timing and baseline.

### How to account for variability across trials and participants
Variability across trials and participants is a key concern. The evidence repeatedly notes that SCRs may overlap and that the waveform can be altered by preceding activity [N1-F1]. This means that trial-to-trial variability can be large, especially when interstimulus intervals are short or when responses overlap. The deconvolution approach is specifically proposed to separate overlapping SCRs into continuous phasic activity, which helps account for trial-level variability [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The practical guide also emphasizes the importance of software-based analysis and time-linking, which helps preserve the timing structure across trials and participants [N4-F3].

The study design should therefore include sufficient trials, a clear response window, and appropriate baseline referencing to capture variability. The evidence also supports the use of model-based methods, such as curve-fitting, to improve timing accuracy and amplitude estimates [N1-F1]. For participants, individual differences in sudomotor firing rate and baseline SC can affect SCR timing, so within-subject normalization or baseline correction may be necessary [N1-F1]. In short, variability should be addressed by using robust detection thresholds, trial-based windows, and decomposition methods that can handle overlapping responses [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R2].

## Interpretation and reporting of SCR timing metrics

### How to interpret latency, amplitude, duration, rise time, and fall time in context
The evidence shows that these metrics should be interpreted as part of a waveform profile rather than in isolation. Latency is defined as the period between stimulus onset and the first significant deviation in the signal, and ER-SCR latency is typically placed within a 1–3 s or 1–5 s window [N2-R1][N1-F1]. Amplitude is the standard trough-to-peak difference and is interpreted as a measure of response intensity [N1-F1][N4-R4]. Rise time is a reported SCR metric and is associated with emotional arousal in the biorxiv study, where higher arousal was linked to shorter ER-SCR rise times [N4-R3]. Duration is indirectly indicated by the predefined response window and by the deconvolution result that phasic activity can average less than 2 seconds [N1-F1]. Fall time is not directly quantified, but the waveform is described as a steep rise and a slow decline, which is important for interpreting the decay phase [N1-F1].

Context matters because the same metric can mean different things depending on stimulus type, task, and participant characteristics. The evidence repeatedly notes that preceding phasic activity can alter the shape of subsequent SCRs, and that emotional arousal changes amplitude and rise time [N1-F1][N4-R3]. Therefore, latency and amplitude should not be interpreted as fixed effects; they are context-dependent indicators of sympathetic arousal [N1-F1][N4-R4].

### Common pitfalls in comparing across studies or conditions
A major pitfall is comparing across studies without accounting for different stimulus windows, detection thresholds, and signal processing pipelines. The evidence shows that ER-SCRs are attributed to a stimulus if latency falls within a predefined window, but different studies may use different windows (e.g., 1–3 s vs. 1–5 s) [N1-F1][N2-R1]. This can inflate or deflate apparent differences. Another pitfall is comparing across conditions without controlling for baseline drift, noise, or movement artifacts [N2-R3][N5-F4]. The same evidence notes that manual correction can introduce subjective bias and that artifact detection remains an ongoing challenge [N5-F4]. This means that observed differences may reflect methodological differences rather than true physiological differences.

The evidence also implies that trial-to-trial variability and individual differences can confound comparisons. SCRs may overlap, and the waveform can be altered by preceding activity, so a single trial may not represent the typical response [N1-F1]. Therefore, direct comparisons across conditions should use consistent windows, thresholds, and processing pipelines, and should report the response window and detection criteria explicitly [N1-F1][N2-R1].

### How to report uncertainty and variability in timing estimates
The evidence supports reporting uncertainty by being explicit about the response window, detection threshold, and processing method. The standard trough-to-peak method uses a minimum amplitude criterion, and the window for attributing SCRs is often 1–3 s or 1–5 s after stimulus onset [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The Biopac guide also notes that latency, SCR amplitude, rise time, size, and onset are reported metrics, which implies that these should be reported with their exact definitions [N4-R1]. The practical guide further emphasizes the need for software-based analysis and time-linking, which helps preserve timing structure across trials and participants [N4-F3].

Variability should be reported using descriptive statistics such as mean, standard deviation, or confidence intervals, and the evidence suggests that decomposition methods can improve accuracy by separating overlapping responses [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The automatic artifact recognition literature also shows that artifact detection can reduce uncertainty by removing contamination [N5-R1][N5-R2]. In reporting, uncertainty can also be conveyed by noting that the waveform may be altered by preceding activity and that manual correction can introduce bias [N1-F1][N5-F4].

In conclusion, SCR timing metrics should be interpreted as context-sensitive indicators of sympathetic arousal, with latency and amplitude being especially sensitive to stimulus timing and participant differences [N1-F1][N4-R4]. Across-study comparisons are risky without consistent windows, thresholds, and processing, while uncertainty and variability can be addressed by explicit reporting of response window, detection criterion, and artifact handling [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-F4].

## Methodological considerations for SCR timing analysis

SCR timing analysis is highly sensitive to detection thresholds, signal processing choices, and artifact handling, all of which can distort timing accuracy and inflate or deflate the apparent response profile [N8].

### Detection thresholds and signal processing choices that affect timing accuracy
The standard trough-to-peak method is central to SCR analysis, but it defines amplitude as the difference between peak and trough and does not account for the declining trails of preceding phasic activity [N8]. This can lead to underestimation of subsequent SCRs, which is a methodological effect and should not be confused with refractory processes [N8]. A minimum amplitude criterion, such as 0.05 μS, is often applied to identify meaningful responses [N8]. The Biopac guide also explicitly lists latency, SCR amplitude, rise time, size, and onset as reported metrics, indicating that timing is not determined in isolation but in conjunction with other waveform features [N8].

This suggests that the choice of decomposition method can alter how timing is extracted. The evidence further notes that curve-fitting methods can improve amplitude and latency estimates compared to standard trough-to-peak methods [N8]. Baseline drift and noise are important because they can obscure the SCR waveform. The standard peak detection method assumes a baseline, and the evidence warns that ignoring preceding trails can produce an artificial attenuation effect [N8]. In short, a true SCR is one that is properly timed relative to a stimulus, has sufficient amplitude, and is not contaminated by baseline drift, noise, or movement artifacts. ## Study design and analysis considerations for SCR timing

SCR timing analysis depends on whether the study is stimulus-locked, within-trial, or between-trial, and each approach has different implications for within-subject and between-subject comparisons [N9].

### Time-locked versus within-trial versus between-trial analysis approaches
Event-related skin conductance responses are traditionally analyzed by comparing the amplitude of individual peaks against a pre-stimulus baseline [N9]. The evidence emphasizes that SCR timing is not uniform across subjects. The waveform is described as stereotyped within-subject but variable across subjects [N9]. This is important because within-subject comparisons can be more reliable than between-subject comparisons if the subject’s baseline and response profile are consistent. The same source also notes that the average firing rate of sudomotor fibers is 0.62 Hz, which is relevant because individual differences in sudomotor activity can produce different SCR timing profiles [N9][N1-F1]. This implies that between-subject comparisons should be cautious about interpreting differences as purely physiological, because they may reflect methodological or individual differences in response timing and baseline.

### How to account for variability across trials and participants
Variability across trials and participants is a key concern. The evidence repeatedly notes that SCRs may overlap and that the waveform can be altered by preceding activity [N9]. This means that trial-to-trial variability can be large, especially when interstimulus intervals are short or when responses overlap. In short, variability should be addressed by using robust detection thresholds, trial-based windows, and decomposition methods that can handle overlapping responses [N9][N3-R1][N3-R2].

## Interpretation and reporting of SCR timing metrics

### How to interpret latency, amplitude, duration, rise time, and fall time in context
The evidence shows that these metrics should be interpreted as part of a waveform profile rather than in isolation. Latency is defined as the period between stimulus onset and the first significant deviation in the signal, and ER-SCR latency is typically placed within a 1–3 s or 1–5 s window [N10][N2-R1]. Amplitude is the standard trough-to-peak difference and is interpreted as a measure of response intensity [N10][N4-R4]. Rise time is a reported SCR metric and is associated with emotional arousal in the biorxiv study, where higher arousal was linked to shorter ER-SCR rise times [N10][N4-R3]. Duration is indirectly indicated by the predefined response window and by the deconvolution result that phasic activity can average less than 2 seconds [N10][N1-F1]. Fall time is not directly quantified, but the waveform is described as a steep rise and a slow decline, which is important for interpreting the decay phase [N10][N1-F1].

Context matters because the same metric can mean different things depending on stimulus type, task, and participant characteristics. The evidence repeatedly notes that preceding phasic activity can alter the shape of subsequent SCRs, and that emotional arousal changes amplitude and rise time [N10][N4-R3]. Therefore, latency and amplitude should not be interpreted as fixed effects; they are context-sensitive indicators of sympathetic arousal [N10][N4-R4].

### Common pitfalls in comparing across studies or conditions
A major pitfall is comparing across studies without accounting for different stimulus windows, detection thresholds, and signal processing pipelines. The evidence shows that ER-SCRs are attributed to a stimulus if latency falls within a predefined window, but different studies may use different windows (e.g., 1–3 s vs. 1–5 s) [N10][N1-F1][N2-R1]. The evidence supports reporting uncertainty by being explicit about the response window, detection threshold, and processing method. In reporting, uncertainty can also be conveyed by noting that the waveform may be altered by preceding activity and that manual correction can introduce bias [N10][N1-F1][N5-F4].

## Conclusion

Overall, typical SCR timing in EDA studies is best understood as a context-sensitive waveform with a steep rise, peak, and slow decline, but its exact timing is influenced by stimulus type, task, and participant characteristics [N7][N10]. Common metrics include latency, amplitude, rise time, and, to a lesser extent, fall time, while duration is often indirectly defined by the response window [N7][N10]. Methodologically, timing accuracy depends on detection thresholds, signal processing choices, and artifact handling, with baseline drift, noise, and movement artifacts being especially important in real-world settings [N8][N10]. In study design, time-locked analysis is standard, but within-trial and between-trial approaches are also used, with important implications for within-subject and between-subject comparisons [N9]. For interpretation and reporting, the evidence supports a careful, explicit approach: report response window, detection threshold, processing method, and uncertainty, and be cautious about comparing across studies or conditions without accounting for methodological and contextual differences [N10]. In short, SCR timing is a powerful but fragile measure, and its analysis should be guided by both physiological understanding and rigorous methodological practice [N7][N8][N9][N10].
